newsitem.title: PERU: Peru launches probe into blame for hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru launches probe into blame for hostage crisis.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori said on Monday a probe was underway into why Peru's security forces failed to prevent Marxist rebels from storming the Japanese ambassador's home and sparking a 69-day hostage siege, Latin America's longest.

"This is in the process of being investigated," Fujimori told reporters on a trip to Peru's eastern jungle. "We cannot speak about culpability yet; there is no trial. But there is responsibility on the part of certain officials and members of the National Police."

He said Peru's intelligence service informed police in the central Huancayo region and Lima that Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels slipped AKM automatic weapons into the capital for a hostage-taking operation and the police high command ordered "corrective measures" on Nov. 15.

His comments confirmed a secret police report obtained by Reuters that showed regional anti-terrorist police warned authorities in Lima weeks before the takeover that the MRTA was planning an assault around Nov. 30.
On Dec. 17, rebels shocked the world by seizing the diplomatic compound and taking hundreds of hostages. All but 72 have been released.
Fujimori spoke hours after a fifth round of hostage talks and the second round between government negotiator Domingo Palermo and MRTA chief Nestor Cerpa.
A statement issued by guarantors overseeing the talks merely said that the two met in a "cordial atmosphere" and broached "important issues."

The statement, read in Spanish by the Vatican's representative, Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, and in English by Canada's ambassador, Anthony Vincent, added that a sixth round of negotiations would be held on Tuesday.
Speaking in the jungle town of Mazamari, Fujimori said talks were in a "preliminary stage" and the two sides had not reached "a base agreement" for formal negotiations to end the crisis.

He denied a report in a Japanese newspaper that Fujimori had agreed to place on the agenda for final negotiations the rebels' main demand of freedom for 400 jailed comrades. The government flatly rejected the idea.
"That is not true," Fujimori said of the report in Mainichi Shimbun. "The government's position is the same."

Cerpa and his deputy, Rolly Rojas, were driven back to the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence in a Red Cross car from a safe house across the street after Monday's meeting, which lasted more than two hours.

When they left the diplomatic compound earlier in the morning, their fellow rebels cheered, broadcast a revolutionary anthem commemorating dead comrades and bellowed defiant slogans. "We are the ones who have taken the Japanese residence. Until death, damn it!" they shouted.
Also at the meeting was Palermo's adviser, Jose Antonio Payet, Red Cross representative and third guarantor Michel Minnig, and the Japanese government's observer, Terusuke Terada.
Talks began on Feb. 11 after weeks of intransigence over the rebels' central demand for the release of jailed comrades.
Among the men still held at the mansion are Fujimori's brother Pedro, two Peruvian ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
